prompt: In `OrderServiceTest`, nothing was stubbed for `books.findByIdForUpdate(3L)`. What does the mock return?
hint: Look at the method's return type.

choices.text: `null`, the default for every object
choices.why: Mockito returns `null` for most object types, but not for `Optional`: it gives an empty one, so code calling `orElseThrow` does not crash with a `NullPointerException`.

choices.text: An empty `Optional`
choices.why: Right. That is why the detour without a stubbing got `BookNotFoundException`: the service treated the empty answer as a book that does not exist.

choices.text: Nothing: the mock throws, because the call was never stubbed
choices.why: A Mockito mock does not refuse an unstubbed call; it answers with an empty value. Only a stubbing whose arguments do not match is refused under strict stubs.

choices.text: The book a previous test stubbed, since the mock is shared
choices.why: `MockitoExtension` creates a fresh mock for every test, so nothing stubbed in one test is visible in the next.

prompt: Why does the first test program `orders.save` with `thenAnswer` rather than `thenReturn`?

choices.text: `thenReturn` cannot return an entity, only plain values
choices.why: `thenReturn` returns any object, entities included; the stubbing of `findByIdForUpdate` returns one.

choices.text: `thenReturn` would call the real `save` of Spring Data
choices.why: No stubbing calls the real method; a mock has no real method behind it. A spy would, and there is none here.

choices.text: The order is created inside `place`, so the test has nothing to hand back in advance
choices.why: Right. The answer runs at the call, takes the order from the arguments, gives it id 7 and returns it.

choices.text: `thenAnswer` makes the test faster because it skips Hibernate
choices.why: Neither choice touches Hibernate: both stub a mock, and the speed is the same.

prompt: The second test ends with `verify(orders, never()).save(any())`. Which statements about that line are true? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: It asks the mock which calls it received during the test
choices.why: Right. A mock records every call, and `verify` reads that record after the fact.

choices.text: It fails the test if `save` was called at all, whatever the argument
choices.why: Right. `any()` matches every argument, and `never()` allows zero calls.

choices.text: It stops the service from calling `save` while the test runs
choices.why: `verify` runs after the call under test and only checks; it changes nothing the service does.

choices.text: It also checks that `books` received no calls
choices.why: It names the mock `orders` and its method `save`, and says nothing about `books`, which was in fact called.

choices.text: A stub alone could not express it
choices.why: Right. A stub only answers calls; whether a call happened is a question for the record a mock keeps.

prompt: Match each kind of test double to what it does.

pairs.right: fills a parameter and is never used
returns answers the test chose in advance
a real object that also records its calls

right_distractors: a copy of the production database

prompt: A test stubs `books.findByIdForUpdate(5L)`, and the service, given an order for book 3, calls `findByIdForUpdate(3L)`. The class uses `MockitoExtension`. What happens?

choices.text: The call returns an empty `Optional` and the test goes on to its assertions
choices.why: That is what an unstubbed method does; here a stubbing exists for the same method with different arguments, and strict stubs refuse that combination.

choices.text: The mock returns the stubbed book anyway, since the method is the same
choices.why: A stubbing matches on its arguments; 5 is not 3, so it does not apply.

choices.text: The test fails with a `PotentialStubbingProblem` before any assertion runs
choices.why: Right. This is the lesson's second detour: Mockito names the call it got and the stubbing it had.

choices.text: Mockito prints a warning and lets the test pass
choices.why: Strict stubs make the mismatch an error, not a warning; the build fails.

prompt: What does `-javaagent:${org.mockito:mockito-core:jar}` in surefire's `argLine` change?

choices.text: It lets Mockito mock final classes, which it could not do before
choices.why: Mockito 5's inline mock maker could already do that by attaching itself; the option changes when the agent arrives, not what it can do.

choices.text: The agent is loaded as the test JVM starts, so Mockito no longer attaches itself mid-run
choices.why: Right, and with nothing attaching, both Mockito's message and the JDK's four warnings disappear.

choices.text: It hides the JDK's warning while Mockito keeps attaching as before
choices.why: That is what `-XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading` would do, and the lesson rejects it for exactly that reason.

choices.text: It makes the tests start faster by sharing Mockito's classes between runs
choices.why: Class data sharing is the JVM's own cache, and the one line left says it now covers fewer classes, not more.

prompt: The goal of `maven-dependency-plugin` that gives every dependency a variable named `groupId:artifactId:type`, holding its jar's path in the local repository, is called `___`.
hint: It runs in the initialize phase.

prompt: After the agent is in the `argLine`, one line remains: `Sharing is only supported for boot loader classes because bootstrap classpath has been appended`. What is it?

choices.text: A sign that the agent failed to load and Mockito is still attaching
choices.why: If Mockito were still attaching, its own message and the four `WARNING:` lines would be back, and they are gone.

choices.text: A test failure Maven reports in a different format
choices.why: All seventeen tests passed in that run; the line comes from the JVM, not from a test.

choices.text: A warning that the agent's jar is too old for JDK 25
choices.why: Nothing in the line mentions a version, and the agent works: the attaching messages are gone.

choices.text: The JVM noting that its class data sharing covers fewer classes, which is harmless
choices.why: Right. The agent adds classes to the boot class path, and the JVM's cache of shared classes then covers less of it.

prompt: A colleague proposes `-XX:+EnableDynamicAgentLoading` in `argLine` instead of the `-javaagent:` option, since "the warnings go away too". What does that leave in place?

choices.text: Mockito still attaching itself in the middle of every run
choices.why: Right. The flag only tells the JDK not to report it; the self-attach the JDK has announced it will stop allowing is still how Mockito gets in.

choices.text: Nothing: the two options are equivalent ways of loading the agent
choices.why: One loads the agent at start; the other permits loading it later. Only the first removes the late attach.

choices.text: The tests failing, because the flag forbids agents
choices.why: The flag does the opposite: it allows dynamic loading, so the tests pass.

choices.text: Mockito's own message, while the JDK's four lines disappear
choices.why: Partly true and not the point: what remains that matters is the late attach itself, which the message is about.

prompt: Match each phase `mvn verify` runs to what happens in it in the bookshop.

pairs.right: the jar is built and repackaged by Boot
failsafe runs the classes named *IT and records the results
failsafe reads the record and fails the build if a test failed

right_distractors: Flyway migrates the bookshop's own database

prompt: Someone names a new class that starts a PostgreSQL container `BookRepositoryTests`. What changes?

choices.text: Nothing, because Maven sees the container and hands the class to failsafe
choices.why: Neither plugin looks inside a class; they choose by name, and `*Tests` is surefire's.

choices.text: Neither plugin runs it, so its tests are silently skipped
choices.why: `*Tests` is one of surefire's patterns, so it does run, just in the wrong place.

choices.text: Surefire runs it with the unit tests, so every `mvn test` needs Docker and starts a container
choices.why: Right. The suffix is the whole switch, and this one puts a slow test into the fast loop.

choices.text: Maven refuses to compile a test class with that suffix
choices.why: The name is legal Java and Maven compiles it; only which plugin runs it depends on the name.

prompt: Why does failsafe only record failures in `integration-test` and fail the build later, in `verify`?

choices.text: Because integration tests are allowed to fail without breaking the build
choices.why: They are not: a failure still fails the build, one phase later.

choices.text: So that the unit tests can run between the two phases
choices.why: The unit tests ran long before, in `test`; nothing of theirs happens after `integration-test`.

choices.text: Because reading the results is slow and is postponed to the end
choices.why: Reading a summary file is quick; the order exists for what has to run between the two.

choices.text: So that `post-integration-test` still runs and stops whatever was started for the tests
choices.why: Right. A server or database started before the tests must be stopped even when they failed.

prompt: Put in order the phases `mvn verify` runs that the lesson's `grep` showed plugins for.
hint: The jar is built before any integration test runs.

prompt: Why does membership of the `docker` group amount to root on that machine?

choices.text: The engine runs as root and does what a member asks, such as start a container that mounts the whole disk
choices.why: Right. The socket is the engine's door, and the group is the key to it.

choices.text: `usermod -aG docker` also adds the user to `sudo`
choices.why: `usermod -aG docker` adds exactly one group, and `id -nG` showed only `ana docker`.

choices.text: The `docker` group is group number 0, the same as root's
choices.why: It is an ordinary group with an ordinary number; the power comes from what the engine does on request.

choices.text: Members can read every file directly, without the engine
choices.why: Membership grants nothing on files by itself; everything goes through the socket, to an engine that runs as root.

prompt: `docker version` prints the `Client` block and then an error, with no `Server` block. What does that say?

choices.text: Docker is not installed
choices.why: Then there would be no `docker` command to print a `Client` block at all.

choices.text: The command is installed and the engine was not reachable
choices.why: Right. The client printed what it knows about itself and failed to reach the server through the socket.

choices.text: The client and the engine have different versions
choices.why: A mismatch would still show both blocks, each with its own version.

choices.text: The `hello-world` image has not been downloaded yet
choices.why: `docker version` uses no image; it only asks the engine about itself.

prompt: Match each message to what it means.

pairs.left: permission denied while trying to connect to the docker API
pairs.right: the engine runs and refused this process

pairs.left: failed to connect to the docker API
Could not find a valid Docker environment
pairs.right: Testcontainers found no engine it could use
Docker Hub's limit on pulls without an account

right_distractors: the image's checksum did not match

prompt: Right after `sudo usermod -aG docker $USER`, `docker ps` answers `permission denied`. Which of these belong to the right way out? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Log out of the VM and log in again
choices.why: Right. A process keeps the groups it started with, and only a new login starts with the new one.

choices.text: Run `id -nG` and look for `docker` in the list
choices.why: Right. It shows the groups of this shell, which is exactly what the engine checks.

choices.text: `sudo chmod 666 /var/run/docker.sock`
choices.why: It hands the engine, and so root, to every account on the machine, and the next restart of the engine undoes it.

choices.text: Run the tests as `sudo mvn verify` from now on
choices.why: Maven would then write files owned by root into `target/` and `~/.m2`, and the group problem is still there for every other command.

prompt: `mvn verify` fails with `DOCKER_HOST unix:///var/run/docker.sock is not listening`, yet the engine is running and `id -nG` in that terminal prints only your own name. What is the cause?

choices.text: The engine listens on another socket, and `DOCKER_HOST` must be set
choices.why: The socket is where Docker's packages put it and the engine is running there; the message's wording misleads.

choices.text: The PostgreSQL image is missing and has to be pulled by hand
choices.why: Testcontainers pulls missing images itself, and it never got as far as asking for one.

choices.text: The socket refused a shell that lacks the `docker` group, and Testcontainers reports that as not listening
choices.why: Right. `docker ps` in the same terminal would say `permission denied`, and a new login fixes both.

choices.text: Failsafe forks its JVM without access to Unix sockets
choices.why: The fork is an ordinary process of your user, with your user's groups; that is the problem here, not a missing ability.

prompt: What does `@ServiceConnection` on the container bean do?

choices.text: It publishes the container's port 5432 on the machine's port 5432
choices.why: Docker publishes it on whatever port is free, 32844 in one run; nothing ties it to 5432 on the machine.

choices.text: It tells Flyway which migrations to apply to the container
choices.why: Flyway reads `db/migration` as always; what changed is the database it connects to.

choices.text: Spring Boot uses the container's address, database, user and password instead of `spring.datasource.*`
choices.why: Right. That is why the test names no port and why Flyway's log shows the container's JDBC URL.

choices.text: It starts Docker Engine if it is not running
choices.why: Nothing in a test starts the engine; without one, the run fails with `Could not find a valid Docker environment`.

prompt: `BookRepositoryIT` uses `@DataJpaTest`. What does that start?

choices.text: The whole application without a web server, like `@SpringBootTest`
choices.why: That is `@SpringBootTest`'s job; the slice leaves out controllers, security filters and services.

choices.text: Only Hibernate, with the schema created from the entities instead of migrations
choices.why: Flyway ran in that slice too: the log shows the three migrations applied to its container.

choices.text: The repositories with an in-memory database that replaces PostgreSQL
choices.why: The log shows the JDBC URL of a PostgreSQL 16 container; nothing in memory took its place.

choices.text: The data source, Flyway, Hibernate and the repositories, each test in a transaction rolled back at its end
choices.why: Right, which is why its context was ready in a fraction of a second.

prompt: In one `mvn verify` of this lesson's bookshop, how many containers from the image `postgres:16-alpine` were started?
hint: One per owner: a context and a test class.

prompt: A build server prints the JNA `restricted method` warning on every build, while your machine printed it once. Neither has `--enable-native-access`. Why the difference?

choices.text: The server runs an older JDK that warns more often
choices.why: The warning exists since JDK 24 and appears the same way on newer ones; the version is not what differs.

choices.text: Each server build starts clean, without `~/.testcontainers.properties`, so the search that loads JNA runs every time
choices.why: Right. Your machine wrote that file after its first successful run and goes straight to the socket since.

choices.text: Docker on the server is a remote engine, which always needs native code
choices.why: Nothing here says the server's engine is remote, and the warning depended on the file, not on where the engine was.

choices.text: Your machine silenced the warning after showing it the first time
choices.why: The JVM has no memory of earlier warnings between runs; something else made the later runs skip the call.

prompt: In the measured `mvn verify`, what took most of the time the integration tests added?

choices.text: Starting the two PostgreSQL containers
choices.why: Each took about 1.3 seconds, the wait for connections included; together, less than half of the context.

choices.text: Downloading the images
choices.why: The images were already on the machine; none of the measured runs downloaded anything.

choices.text: Starting the whole application context for `BookshopApplicationIT`
choices.why: Right: 6.2 seconds in that run, against under 0.4 for the persistence slice.

choices.text: Flyway applying the three migrations
choices.why: Flyway reported an execution time of a few hundredths of a second for all three.

prompt: Put in order what happens during `BookshopApplicationIT`, from the moment the test JVM needs a database until nothing of the run is left.
items: Testcontainers starts Ryuk and keeps a connection open to it
the PostgreSQL container starts, its 5432 published on a free port
Testcontainers waits until PostgreSQL accepts connections
Flyway migrates the empty schema to version 3
the JVM exits and Ryuk, after a few seconds, removes itself

prompt: You add `CatalogueIT`, annotated exactly like `BookshopApplicationIT`: `@SpringBootTest`, `@ActiveProfiles("test")`, `@Import(TestcontainersConfiguration.class)`. How many extra PostgreSQL containers does `mvn verify` start for it?

choices.text: One, because every test class gets its own container
choices.why: That is the `static @Container` field's behaviour; this class uses the bean, which belongs to a context.

choices.text: None: Spring reuses the cached context, and the container bean comes with it
choices.why: Right. Same configuration, same context, same database, and no extra seconds of context start either.

choices.text: Two, one for the context and one for Ryuk
choices.why: Ryuk is not PostgreSQL, and one Ryuk serves the whole run.

choices.text: It depends on whether Ryuk removed the first container in between
choices.why: The first container lives as long as its context, which stays cached for the whole run; Ryuk only acts when the JVM is gone.

prompt: A change to `findTitlesByAuthor`'s `@Query` makes it return the right titles in the wrong order. Which of these would catch it? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: `BookRepositoryIT`
choices.why: Right. It runs the real query on PostgreSQL and asserts the exact order with `containsExactly`.

choices.text: `mvn verify`
choices.why: Right. It runs `BookRepositoryIT`, records the failure and fails the build at `verify`.

choices.text: `mvn test`
choices.why: It stops before `package` and never runs a class named `*IT`.

choices.text: `OrderServiceTest`
choices.why: It mocks the repositories, so no query of theirs ever runs in it.

choices.text: `BookshopApplicationIT`
choices.why: It starts everything and counts the books; it never calls this query, so the order is invisible to it.
